https://www.walesonline.co.uk/lifestyle/.text: Channel 4 's Taskmaster is returning for a new series in a matter of weeks and the confirmation comes after Greg Davies admitted how his co-host "genuinely annoys" him. Welshman Greg, who is from St Asaph, will return to Channel 4 alongside Alex Horne on Thursday, September 3 for series 22. But recently, the 58-year-old stand-up comedian admitted there are things his co-host does that "genuinely annoys" him. Greg told Metro: "I think he deliberately sits down and thinks: 'I know how to get Greg into character, and it's to properly wind him up.' He says things that have no structure, punchline [or] comic premise, and it genuinely annoys me. "[The scoring] is my revenge. It's the little things he doesn't like. When I give two contestants the same score, if you look into his eyes, his little brain is on fire with rage because he wants things put into boxes." But hopefully there won't be too much squabbling between them when the series returns with a number of famous names among the cast including Peep Show's Isy Suttie, Doctor Who's Matt Lucas, ventriloquist comedian Nina Conti, stand-up comedian Chloe Petts and The Bad Guys' Richard Ayoade. The tasks this time around will see the celebs "crawl through secret tunnels, look for faces on toast, go on holiday with shoes and make interesting use of their armpits", reports Digital Spy. In an interview with Polygon in June, Greg said their "roles have become organically defined, rather than in those first few seasons — sorry, series — when we sat down and decided what the dynamics should be and how we should respond". He added: "They were almost 'eggy' in comparison to where we are now, which is that we both know the limits of our roles and what the dynamic is. It feels a lot more fun now, to be honest, because we know the [Taskmaster] world and the limitations to the world." Taskmaster has been expanding across the globe in recent years, with the YouTube channel almost doubling its views across 2025. Earlier this year, it was announced that a Polish version is on the way, which is the 14th international version. The upcoming season of Taskmaster UK will return to the UK on Thursday, September 3 at 9pm - its usual time slot - and will then drop an hour later on the Taskmaster YouTube channel around the world. Taskmaster returns to Channel 4 on September 3

https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-insti.text: BRUSSELS — The European Union institutions kept calm and carried on regulating on Friday, as many other parts of the world muttered at their computers over a massive digital outage at U.S. tech leader Microsoft. The European Commission, Council of the EU and European Parliament were able to carry on business as usual, with systems remaining largely unaffected. Microsoft’s global outage , which disrupted Outlook, Teams and Copilot started on Thursday, with internet traffic monitoring site Downdetector reporting issues in at least 74 countries. The tracker logged nearly 140,000 reports of Outlook problems at its peak. Advertisement Advertisement Microsoft on Friday morning said recovery was still uneven . "At this time, we have no evidence of malicious activity associated with this incident. We will continue to treat this with urgency until full mitigation," it said. At the European Commission “the impact ... is very limited and does not affect our operations,” spokesperson Thomas Regnier told POLITICO. He said the outage had a “minor impact on a limited number of applications, such as the slowness of SharePoint.” Outlook and Teams were “fully operational,” Regnier said. The Council of the EU, which gathers representatives of national governments, also carried on work: Outlook and Teams were “working on our side,” a Council official told POLITICO, declining to give more details on the institution’s IT setup. The Parliament's press service said in a statement to POLITICO that it was unaffected and was monitoring the situation as a precaution. The outage is exposing the reliance of companies and governments on Microsoft services — an issue that has also been a longstanding concern in Europe among proponents of keeping more control over IT and digital infrastructure. In October last year, a similar outage of Amazon Web Services servers prompted immediate calls for Europe to boost its tech sovereignty . Advertisement Advertisement Efforts to move away from American tech providers got a boost in the past two years due to concerns that the U.S. administration of Donald Trump could disrupt digital services in Europe for political gain. Governments across Europe have launched a wide range of initiatives to boost local competitors to U.S. Big Tech and build public services on homegrown platforms. One example is the government of Germany’s northernmost state of Schleswig-Holstein, which in 2025 moved about 40,000 mailboxes from Microsoft Exchange and Outlook to open-source alternatives to reduce their reliance on U.S. tech. The state's digitalization minister, Dirk Schrödter, said in a comment to POLITICO on Friday that disruptions like the Microsoft outage “must be taken very seriously,” whether the state uses open-source software or products from individual providers. “We must be able to intervene ourselves at any time if problems arise,” he said. Francesca Micheletti contributed to this report.

https://www.ewtnnews.com/world/us/theolo.text: Theology of the body meets psychology: Catholics seek healing through JPII’s personalism Catholics gathered to explore how St. John Paul II’s understanding of the person can integrate with psychological science to address anxiety and the search for lasting love and healing. Christopher West speaks at the Summit of Integration conference in Dallas on Oct. 22, 2026. | Credit: Amira Abuzeid/EWTN News By Amira Abuzeid Follow + November 2, 2026 at 7:00 AM ET In a culture marked by rising rates of anxiety and a loss of meaning, a growing number of Catholics are seeking ways to promote human flourishing by integrating the best in psychological science with the personalist philosophy of St. John Paul II. Catholics gathered at the CatholicPsych Institute’s Summit of Integration from Oct. 20–23 in Dallas. Its founder, Greg Bottaro, whose work centers on the integration of St. John Paul II’s teachings on the meaning and purpose of the body with the practice of psychology, told attendees that “St. John Paul II has written more for psychologists than any other psychologist in the last 150 years.” “John Paul II didn’t use the language of psychology in his theology of the body , but everything he talked about was relatable to the field,” Bottaro told EWTN News. “Faith, reason, and science all come together in his work.” The theology of the body teaches that the human person is a unity of body and soul, created male and female in the image of God and called to communion through the sincere gift of self. The body has a “nuptial” or spousal meaning: It expresses the person and is ordered toward loving self-gift, which is fully realized either in the permanent, exclusive, and life-giving union of marriage or in the celibate gift of self for the kingdom. Speakers at the conference, which was timed to coincide with St. John Paul II’s feast day on Oct. 22, tied the saint’s writings to their own work and personal lives. A love that is ‘stronger than death’ Christopher West, a Catholic author and educator who specializes in the theology of the body, gave an address called “My Interior Journey with St. John Paul II.” West said the saint’s writings helped him make sense of a yearning that began when he was a child, a yearning that he explained was for a love that would never end. He described this yearning as beginning with an innocent crush on a girl in his third grade class, but as he grew up, it led him to a disordered view of sexuality and the body: “I wanted a beauty; I wanted a joy; I wanted happiness that lasts forever, that does not die.” “The Church calls this yearning eros,” the Greek word for romantic love, he said. “Eros cries out for a love that is ‘stronger than death,’” he continued, quoting the Song of Songs in the Old Testament. “Christianity is an invitation to a wedding feast that corresponds to that cry of the heart,” he said. St. John Paul II taught that “Christianity is not redemption from the body and sexuality. It is the redemption of the body and sexuality. Christ came into the world, not to condemn those whose eros is distorted, but to untwist it.” “The most disastrous mistake of Christians is to view sexuality as trash and throw it away rather than redeem it,” he continued. “We have three choices with eros: Repress it, aim it at finite pleasure, or, by the grace of God, learn how to aim our desire for the infinite toward the infinite.” He said he sees St. John Paul II not primarily as a theologian but as a spiritual father whose writings helped him confront his own fear of death. “This boundless demand of eros expresses the basic problem of human existence: The heart demands infinity but cannot grant it. It claims eternity but is bound by death,” West continued. “Our deepest fear is staring into our own death.” A slide during Christopher West's address at the Summit of Integration in Dallas on Oct. 22, 2026, showing a young West with St. John Paul II. | Credit: Amira Abuzeid/EWTN News “John Paul II truly fathered me,” West said. “This is the gift of this man in my life: He has helped me face my deepest fear and gave me courage.” West said he needed that courage to confront difficulties that fear caused in his 31-year marriage to his wife, Wendy, who sat in the front row as he spoke. He said he had discovered “deep, unconscious wounds of rejection” he’d received from his brother during his childhood but that ultimately came from a fear of death that led him to “rejecting the true heart of my wife.” “When I have caused you so much sorrow and suffering, it’s because I wanted you to do something you couldnʼt possibly do for me, which is to take away my fear of death,” he said. “I wanted you to take that existential threat away.” “And weʼre aging, haven’t you noticed?” he asked her, laughing. “Weʼre in our late 50s, and all the gray hair is a reminder that weʼre dying; weʼre all on this conveyor belt, and weʼre all gonna fall off.” An ‘inheritance to life’ In his keynote, Bottaro repeatedly returned to the idea that Christians receive an “inheritance to life” from God rather than an inheritance of fear and death. “The inheritance of life, the legacy of life, of the Resurrection is the answer to the deepest fear in the human heart: death,” he said, pointing to St. John Paul II’s admonition to “‘Be not afraid!’” Bottaro also described the saint as a spiritual father who shaped his life. He spoke of a visit to Poland during a time he was struggling with discouragement in his work. He was sitting at the kitchen table where a young Karol Wojtyla (John Paul II) had discovered his father dead. As Bottaro sat, he said he felt “John Paul II just put his arms around me,” after which he was able to return to his professional efforts with a renewed purpose. He spent the next five years writing “The Personalist Cure,” a book that integrates the saint’s theological teachings with psychology. It was released during the conference, on St. John Paul II’s feast day. Bottaro said the book is a manual for how to understand healing and mental health through a Catholic lens and is intended for anybody studying mental health or human formation. CatholicPsych Institute founder Greg Bottaro speaks at the Summit of Integration in Dallas on Oct. 22, 2026. | Credit: Photo courtesy of the CatholicPsych Institute Michelle Gardiner, a mother of four who attended the conference, told EWTN News the summit “surrounded me with the reality John Paul II gave his life to: Authentic healing begins with reverencing and protecting the inviolable gift of myself and every other human person.” “We inadvertently turn away from God, the supreme lover who created us for delight, when we reject the gift because of interpersonal wounding,” she said. “John Paul II knew this: Authentic human flourishing requires receiving and protecting the inviolable gift of the human person.” Amira Abuzeid Follow + Amira Abuzeid is a senior editor at EWTN News with a special interest in bioethics, technology, theology, and religion in public life.
